issues.legal_issue: A successor may satisfy the ownership and letting requirements for expedited recovery of a dwelling when the property was owned in the predecessor’s name and let by the predecessor.
material_facts: The government officer was required to vacate government-provided residential accommodation because he owned a dwelling.
The dwelling had stood in his deceased father’s name, and his father had let the relevant premises to the tenant.
The officer claimed through his father as an heir.
issues.conclusion: Ownership inherited from the predecessor, together with the predecessor’s letting of the premises, satisfies the ownership and letting requirements for this recovery procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14A(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, is to be read according to its purpose and practical substance. The requirement that premises be owned by the officer and let by him is met when he succeeds to the ownership and landlord position of a predecessor who owned the premises in his own name and let them.

rule.if: government_employee_recovery_proceeding and required_to_vacate_official_housing and inherited_dwelling_from_predecessor and dwelling_stood_in_predecessors_name and predecessor_directly_let_dwelling

predicates.government_employee_recovery_proceeding: The proceeding seeks expedited recovery of a dwelling by a government employee required to leave government-provided housing.
predicates.required_to_vacate_official_housing: The government employee was required to vacate official residential accommodation.
predicates.inherited_dwelling_from_predecessor: The government employee succeeded to the dwelling through a predecessor.
predicates.dwelling_stood_in_predecessors_name: The dwelling was held in the predecessor’s name.
predicates.predecessor_directly_let_dwelling: The predecessor directly let the dwelling to a tenant.

issues.definition: When an employee in this kind of proceeding must leave official housing and inherits a dwelling held in the predecessor’s name that the predecessor directly let, the inherited ownership satisfies the ownership and letting requirements.

issues.legal_issue: A person who receives rent as the tenant’s recognized landlord may qualify as a landlord under rent-control law even when acting for a deceased owner’s estate or other persons.
material_facts: The deceased owner had let the premises to the tenant.
After the owner’s death, the tenant paid rent to the respondent, who initially received it on behalf of the deceased owner’s estate and later issued receipts in his own name.
The respondent functioned as the person receiving rent from the tenant.
issues.conclusion: The respondent qualified as the landlord for purposes of the rent-control proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(e) and 2(l) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, define landlord and tenant by reference to the receipt or entitlement to receive rent and the person by whom or on whose behalf rent is payable. In rent-control proceedings before a special tribunal, the practical relationship between the rent collector and the tenant governs; concepts of estoppel or the Transfer of Property Act need not be imported inflexibly.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_paid_rent_to_claimant: The tenant paid rent to the person claiming the right to bring the eviction proceeding.
predicates.claimant_received_rent_as_recognized_lan: The person claiming eviction received rent in a capacity recognized by the tenant as landlord, including on behalf of an estate or other persons.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, a claimant who receives rent from the tenant as the recognized landlord qualifies as a landlord.

issues.legal_issue: A co-owner who is the acknowledged landlord may seek eviction without joining the other co-owners when they do not oppose the proceeding.
material_facts: The respondent was one of the deceased owner’s heirs and a co-owner of the premises.
The respondent collected rent from the tenant as part of the body of landlords.
The other co-heirs were joined at the High Court stage, and the record did not show that they opposed the respondent’s claim.
issues.conclusion: The respondent’s status as a co-owner and the absence of the other co-owners at the initial stage did not disentitle him from suing for eviction.
issues.legal_principle: A co-owner owns every part of the composite property along with the other co-owners and is not merely a fractional owner. Under Sri Ram Pasricha, a co-owner who is also the acknowledged landlord need not establish sole ownership to sue for eviction. The Court left open the situation in which other co-owners oppose the eviction.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and claimant_is_co_owner and claimant_is_acknowledged_landlord and other_co_owners_do_not_oppose

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.claimant_is_co_owner: The person bringing the proceeding owns the premises together with other co-owners.
predicates.claimant_is_acknowledged_landlord: The tenant recognizes the person bringing the proceeding as a landlord.
predicates.other_co_owners_do_not_oppose: The other co-owners do not oppose the requested eviction.

issues.definition: A co-owner who is recognized as landlord may seek eviction without joining the other co-owners when they do not oppose the claim.

issues.legal_issue: The expedited recovery right available to a government employee required to vacate official housing cannot be used to recover more than one dwelling from different tenants.
material_facts: The government officer had been required to vacate his official residential accommodation.
Using that ground, he had already recovered another dwelling from a tenant in the same building and kept it vacant.
He then sought to recover the appellant’s separate dwelling using the same ground.
issues.conclusion: Having recovered one dwelling under that ground, the respondent could not use it again to evict the appellant from another dwelling.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14A(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, read with its proviso, provides an accelerated remedy to restore a government employee to residential accommodation and does not confer a right to recover more than one dwelling house. The proviso allows the landlord to choose which dwelling to recover; the right is exhausted upon recovery of one dwelling.

rule.if: government_employee_recovery_proceeding and required_to_vacate_official_housing and already_recovered_one_dwelling_on_that_ground and seeks_another_dwelling_on_same_ground

predicates.government_employee_recovery_proceeding: The proceeding seeks expedited recovery of a dwelling by a government employee required to leave government-provided housing.
predicates.required_to_vacate_official_housing: The government employee was required to vacate official residential accommodation.
predicates.already_recovered_one_dwelling_on_that_g: The landlord has already recovered possession of one dwelling using the same requirement to vacate official housing as the ground.
predicates.seeks_another_dwelling_on_same_ground: The landlord seeks possession of a separate dwelling from another tenant using that same ground.

issues.definition: If a government employee required to leave official housing has already recovered one dwelling on that ground and seeks another on the same ground, the employee cannot recover the additional dwelling under it.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to a successor’s claim based on an unproved will cannot succeed as a bare objection lacking support in the record.
material_facts: The respondent claimed an interest in the premises under his deceased father’s will.
The tenant argued that the will had not been proved and that he had not had an opportunity to challenge it.
The other heirs were parties in the High Court, and the record did not show that they objected to the respondent’s claim to the relevant floor under the will.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the challenge because it was an objection without a realistic foundation in the record.
issues.legal_principle: An objection unsupported by any realistic foundation in the record is not to be entertained merely for the sake of procedural punctiliousness.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and tenant_challenges_successors_claim_under_will and other_heirs_are_before_court and record_shows_no_heir_objection and challenge_has_no_realistic_foundation

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_challenges_successors_claim_under: The tenant disputes the claimant’s asserted entitlement under a will.
predicates.other_heirs_are_before_court: The other heirs whose interests may be affected are before the court.
predicates.record_shows_no_heir_objection: The record does not show that the other heirs object to the claimant’s asserted entitlement.
predicates.challenge_has_no_realistic_foundation: The tenant’s challenge has no factual support in the record beyond the bare assertion that the will has not been proved.

issues.definition: When a tenant’s challenge to a successor’s claim under a will lacks record support and the other heirs before the court do not object, the unsupported challenge is rejected.
